name: MATCH
description: MATCH searches for a specified value in a range and returns its relative position. It's the search engine that powers INDEX/MATCH — the most flexible lookup combination in Excel.
tldr: MATCH finds where a value sits in a range and returns its position number. It's the 'finder' half of INDEX/MATCH — MATCH locates the row, INDEX retrieves the value at that row.

parameters.name: lookup_value
parameters.description: The value you want to find in the lookup_array.

parameters.name: lookup_array
parameters.description: The single-row or single-column range to search through.

parameters.name: match_type
parameters.description: 0 = exact match, 1 = largest value ≤ lookup (requires ascending sort), -1 = smallest value ≥ lookup (requires descending sort). Default is 1.

basicExample.description: Find the position of 'East' in a list of regions
basicExample.explanation: This searches column A for the exact text 'East' and returns 3 (meaning it's in the 3rd cell of the range A2:A10).

advancedExamples.title: INDEX/MATCH lookup
advancedExamples.description: Use MATCH to find a row position, then INDEX to retrieve the corresponding value
advancedExamples.explanation: MATCH finds where E2's value appears in column A. INDEX then retrieves the corresponding value from column C at that position.

advancedExamples.title: Two-way lookup with double MATCH
advancedExamples.description: Find both the row and column positions using two MATCH functions
advancedExamples.explanation: First MATCH finds the row by searching column A. Second MATCH finds the column by searching row 1. INDEX retrieves the value at the intersection.

advancedExamples.title: Approximate match for closest value
advancedExamples.description: Find the closest matching value in a sorted list
advancedExamples.explanation: With match_type 1 (approximate), MATCH finds the largest value ≤ 85 in the ascending-sorted list.

howItWorks: MATCH scans through the lookup_array and compares each cell to the lookup_value. For exact match (match_type=0), it looks for an identical value and returns its position. For approximate match (match_type=1), it finds the largest value that is ≤ the lookup value — the array must be sorted ascending. For match_type=-1, it finds the smallest value ≥ the lookup value — the array must be sorted descending. The position returned is relative to the start of the range, not the worksheet row number.

howToSteps.name: Identify the value to find
howToSteps.text: Decide what you're searching for — a specific text, number, or cell reference.

howToSteps.name: Select the search range
howToSteps.text: Choose a single-row or single-column range to search through.

howToSteps.name: Choose match type
howToSteps.text: 0 for exact match (most common), 1 for approximate ascending, -1 for approximate descending.

howToSteps.name: Enter the formula
howToSteps.text: Type =MATCH(lookup_value, search_range, match_type) to get the position number.

limitations: MATCH only searches one-dimensional ranges (single row or single column).
For approximate match, the data must be sorted correctly — wrong sort order gives wrong results.
MATCH returns only the first match. If duplicates exist, you only get the position of the first occurrence.
MATCH returns a position number, not a value — you need INDEX to get the actual data.

commonErrors.cause: No match found in the lookup_array for exact match mode
commonErrors.fix: Check that the value exists in the range, or use IFNA/MATCH to handle missing values.

commonErrors.cause: Using match_type 1 or -1 on unsorted data
commonErrors.fix: For approximate match, the lookup_array must be sorted: ascending for match_type 1, descending for match_type -1.

commonErrors.cause: lookup_array is not a 1D range (contains multiple rows AND columns)
commonErrors.fix: MATCH requires a single row or single column. If you need 2D search, use XLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH with separate row/column searches.

googleSheetsEquivalent.description: MATCH works identically in Google Sheets with the same syntax and behavior.
googleSheetsEquivalent.notes: Google Sheets MATCH is fully compatible with Excel MATCH. Combined with INDEX, it's the primary lookup method in Sheets since XLOOKUP isn't available.

faq.question: What's the difference between MATCH match_type 0, 1, and -1?
faq.answer: 0 = exact match only. 1 = approximate, finds largest value ≤ lookup (requires ascending sort). -1 = approximate, finds smallest value ≥ lookup (requires descending sort). Always use 0 unless you specifically need approximate matching.

faq.question: Can MATCH search a 2D range?
faq.answer: No. MATCH only works on single-row or single-column ranges. For 2D lookups, use two MATCH functions (one for rows, one for columns) combined with INDEX.

faq.question: Is MATCH faster than VLOOKUP?
faq.answer: For exact match (match_type=0), MATCH and VLOOKUP have similar performance. However, INDEX/MATCH can be more efficient because you're only searching one column, not an entire table.

faq.question: Can MATCH find the last occurrence?
faq.answer: For the last match in a column, use =MATCH(2, 1/(A2:A100=value), 1) as a workaround. XLOOKUP's search_mode=-1 is cleaner for this.
